facts_from_discussion: Petitioner did not introduce credible evidence or show that he maintained required records so as to shift the burden of proof.

The documentary record establishes that during 2021 petitioner made transfers from his E*Trade IRA to his E*Trade brokerage account and to his Wells Fargo account, some in cash and some in stock: cash transfers to the Wells Fargo account of $37,460; cash transfers to the E*Trade brokerage account of $120,013; and stock transfers to the E*Trade brokerage account of $72,384; total $229,857.
The Form 1099-R issued by Morgan Stanley lists the total distributions as $229,856.80 (rounded to $229,857).

Petitioner raised no reasonable dispute about the accuracy of the Form 1099-R and supplied no evidence that E*Trade took his money or reported false distributions; the documentary record confirms the accuracy of Morgan Stanley's reporting.
Cash transfers to the Wells Fargo account: $35,000 on January 26, 2021; $1,460 on August 13, 2021; and $1,000 on October 5, 2021, described as ACH withdrawals from account ending 1601.
Cash transfers to the E*Trade brokerage account (ending 1455): $55,000 and $65,000 on January 26, 2021, and $13 on December 23, 2021.
Stock transfers from the IRA to the brokerage account: $33,266 on May 25, 2021; $26,400 on November 1, 2021; $12,718 on December 23, 2021; the shares were mostly sold shortly afterward in 2021.
The consolidated Form 1099 for the brokerage account shows these shares sold during 2021, and share counts align with the IRA statements.
Petitioner supplied no evidence that the transferred stock came from a source other than his E*Trade IRA and had no comprehensible answer at trial.
At trial petitioner acknowledged he had an E*Trade brokerage account and IRA and moved money and shares back and forth.
The court found that petitioner forgot that his E*Trade IRA account number changed in 2023 from 1601 to 2205.
At trial petitioner confirmed that he had not attained age 59 1/2 during 2021, and he does not contend that any other section 72(t)(2) exception applies.
For 2021 petitioner reported tax of $20,528; the court found his correct tax was [REDACTED AMOUNT].

Petitioner does not dispute supervisory approval; written approval on May 20, 2024 preceded the August 2, 2024 notice (first communication of the penalty) and was given while the supervisor retained discretion; appeal lies to the Ninth Circuit.
The court did not find credible petitioner's testimony that he did not know where the transferred assets came from.
Petitioner is an experienced aerospace engineer; the court did not believe he misunderstood the tax law, and any misunderstanding would not have been reasonable.
The court found petitioner did not show reasonable cause and good faith.
